title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
AI systems were used to generate a fabricated interview article that impersonated a real financial journalist and central bank official to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. The system created text that mimicked the style and credibility of legitimate financial journalism, deployed without human verification before publication. This is a case of impersonation and false assertion of fact at scale: the interview never occurred, the statements were invented, and the platform was not licensed to operate.

The failure occurred in the deployment stage, where generative AI was used to create convincing fraudulent content without the checks that would catch fabrication. Detecting this required recognition that the interview did not match public records of real conversations, or verification that the quoted individuals had actually made those statements. According to regulators, this type of AI-generated impersonation fraud has become common enough to report as a trend, though it is not established whether the systems themselves were designed for fraud or repurposed by bad actors after legitimate deployment.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article featured a fabricated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The article never happened but was created using artificial intelligence technology. According to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, this type of scam is becoming increasingly common and sophisticated as generative AI makes fraudulent content more convincing.

ASIC reports that investment scams surged significantly, with regulators removing 19,400 schemes last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent, while fake investment platforms increased 151 percent. Prominent Australians including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are frequently impersonated in these schemes. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
